body_ar:
من أعظم المتون في مذهب مالك رحمه الله مختصر خليل بن إسحاق، وقد نظمه أحد العلماء نظماً بديعاً جعل أوله في علم العقائد السلفية مما رجع إليه الإمام الأشعري رحمه الله، وبين يديك شرح مقدمة النظم.
فضل علم التوحيد:
بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين، والصلاة والسلام على نبينا محمد وعلى آله وصحبه أجمعين، ثم أما بعد: فقد سبق أن قلنا: إن علم التوحيد هو من أفضل العلوم ولم نقل هو أفضل العلوم، مع أن كثيراً من الذين ألفوا فيه يقولون: هو أفضل العلوم كما قال المقري: وأفضل العلوم بالإطلاق علـم به معرفة الخـلاق لكن يجاب عن هذا: بأن هذا العلم ليس وحده هو الذي به معرفة الخلاق، بل علم التفسير كذلك، وعلم القراءات كذلك، وعلم الحديث كذلك، فمعرفة الخلاق لا تكون إلا بهذه العلوم مجتمعة، كما ذكرنا سابقاً في قضية القرآن وتناوله لكل هذه العلوم، فلذلك لا نجزم بأنه أفضل العلوم على الإطلاق؛ لأن هذه العلوم تكليفياً في مرتبة واحدة، ما يجب منها عيناً يجب في الجميع وما يجب كفاية يجب في الجميع، ويصعب علينا أن نضع مسطرة لها بحسب التفاوت في الفضل، بل نقول: هو من أفضل العلوم، ويكفينا هذا، حتى لا نجازف ونقول على الله بغير علم، فمعرفة الله ليست فقط بهذا العلم، بل تدخل في التفسير، وفي القراءات، وفي الحديث، وفي شرح الحديث، وفي كثير من العلوم الأخرى التي سنذكرها. ...
body_en:
*[Site synopsis]* Among the greatest base texts in the school of Malik, may God have mercy on him, is the Mukhtaṣar of Khalil ibn Ishaq. One of the scholars put it into verse in an exquisite versification, making its opening section on the science of the creed of the early generations — of that to which Imam al-Ashʿari, may God have mercy on him, returned. What is before you is the commentary on the introduction to that versification.

## The merit of the science of the oneness of God

In the name of God, the All-Merciful, the Mercy-Giving. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds, and blessing and peace upon our Prophet Muhammad and upon his family and his Companions all together. And now, to proceed: we have already said that the science of the oneness of God (tawḥīd) is among the most excellent of the sciences — we did not say that it is the most excellent of the sciences — even though many of those who have written on it do say that it is the most excellent of the sciences, as al-Maqqari said:

*And the most excellent of the sciences, taken without qualification, is a science by which the Creator is known.*

But an answer is given to this: that this science is not the only one by which the Creator is known. The science of Qur'anic exegesis (tafsīr) is such a science too, and so is the science of the canonical readings of the Qur'an (qirāʾāt), and so is the science of hadith. Knowledge of the Creator comes about only through these sciences taken together — as we mentioned earlier concerning the Qur'an and its taking up all of these sciences. For this reason we do not assert categorically that it is the most excellent of the sciences without qualification, because these sciences, as regards what they lay upon a person (taklīf), stand at one single level: what among them is individually obligatory (farḍ ʿayn) is individually obligatory across them all, and what is communally obligatory (farḍ kifāyah) is communally obligatory across them all. It is hard for us to lay a measuring rule across them according to a gradation in merit. Rather we say: it is among the most excellent of the sciences — and that suffices us, so that we do not take a risk and say of God what we do not know. For knowledge of God is not through this science only; it enters into exegesis, into the canonical readings, into hadith, into the explanation of hadith, and into many of the other sciences which we shall mention. …

flags.context: the record breaks off and the full text sits behind a download
options: render with an excerpt banner and link the .doc
flags.note: Excerpt only, style guide section 9. It breaks off on an ellipsis after the first announced section, at the point where the Sheikh promises to name the other sciences. Unusually for this run, the argument the excerpt does contain is complete and ends in his own conclusion. The complete text sits behind /medias/doc/L-34.doc. The English ends exactly where the Arabic ends and completes nothing. Must not be rendered as a whole lesson.

flags.arabic: الفقرة الافتتاحية مقابل ما بعد العنوان الفرعي
flags.context: the synopsis paragraph against the transcribed opening of the lesson
options: mark the synopsis as the site's own and the remainder as the Sheikh's words
present the whole record as the Sheikh's words
flags.note: The record has two authors. The first paragraph is a synopsis written by the site — it speaks about the lesson and its subject in the third person and does not begin with the opening formula. Everything from the section heading onward is transcribed speech in the Sheikh's own voice. The site must not present the synopsis as his words.

flags.context: the formula introducing each quoted line of the versified creed being commented on
options: keep 'the Sheikh' unresolved and record the ambiguity
read it as the author of the versified text, distinct from the lecturer
read it as Sheikh al-Dedew quoting his own verse
flags.note: The referent of 'الشيخ' cannot be settled from the served text, and getting it wrong would misattribute a creedal formulation. These lessons are a commentary on a versified creed (nazm): the transcriber introduces each base-text line with 'the Sheikh, may God preserve him, said', then the commentary follows. 'حفظه الله' is used of the living, which fits Sheikh al-Dedew himself — in which case he is both the author of the verse and its commentator — but the formula is also the ordinary way a transcriber marks the author of a base text. The English leaves 'the Sheikh' unresolved exactly as the Arabic does. The Sheikh's office can settle it in one answer, and it should be settled before publication, because the bracketed verse and the prose around it would then carry different attributions.

flags.arabic: وأفضل العلوم بالإطلاق / أفضل العلوم على الإطلاق
flags.context: al-Maqqari's line, and the Sheikh's refusal of it
flags.note: A glossary homonym on which the whole argument turns. 'إطلاق' is the noun of 'مطلق', which the glossary fixes as 'unqualified' in legal theory; that is exactly the sense here, and it must not slide into 'absolutely' as a mere intensifier. The Sheikh's point is precisely about qualification: he accepts the claim in a qualified form ('among the most excellent') and refuses it in its unqualified form. An English that renders 'بالإطلاق' as 'absolutely' turns a distinction into an emphasis and destroys the argument.

flags.arabic: لأن هذه العلوم تكليفياً في مرتبة واحدة، ما يجب منها عيناً يجب في الجميع وما يجب كفاية يجب في الجميع
flags.context: the reason the Sheikh gives for refusing the unqualified claim
options: as regards what they lay upon a person (taklīf), they stand at one level; what is individually obligatory in one is individually obligatory across them all
in terms of legal obligation they are of one rank
flags.note: The load-bearing sentence of the record and the one most easily flattened. Three fixed terms are in play and all three are in the glossary: 'تكليف', what the law lays upon a responsible person; 'فرض عين', individually obligatory; 'فرض كفاية', communally obligatory, discharged on behalf of all if some perform it. The argument is that the sciences cannot be ranked by merit because they are indistinguishable in their standing under the law — whichever portion of one is individually obligatory, the same holds of the others. Collapsing 'عيناً' and 'كفاية' into a single 'obligatory' would remove the argument entirely.

flags.arabic: علم العقائد السلفية مما رجع إليه الإمام الأشعري
flags.context: the site's synopsis, describing the base text's creed section
options: the creed of the early generations, of that to which Imam al-Ashʿari returned
Salafi creed, being what Imam al-Ashʿari came back to
the creed of the forebears, which al-Ashʿari adopted in the end
flags.note: A compressed and contested claim, in the site's words and not the Sheikh's. It asserts that al-Ashʿari returned in the end to the creed of the early generations — a well-known and disputed position about the man's final doctrine, and one that different currents cite for opposite purposes. 'السلفية' is rendered 'of the early generations' rather than transliterated as 'Salafi', because the English word now names a modern movement and would import an anachronism into a sentence about the tenth century. The claim is translated exactly and resolved nowhere.

flags.arabic: حتى لا نجازف ونقول على الله بغير علم
flags.context: the Sheikh's closing reason for the weaker claim
options: so that we do not take a risk and say of God what we do not know
so as not to venture and speak about God without knowledge
flags.note: The clause states the Sheikh's methodological reason for preferring the weaker formulation, and it is the reason a translator of this corpus should read twice: he declines to assert what he cannot establish. Rendered plainly; 'القول على الله بغير علم' is a Qur'anic idiom for making claims about God without warrant, unmarked here as a citation and left unmarked in the English.

translator_notes: One of a run of fifteen records, IDs 707-721, in the written-creed section, all uploaded on 9 and 10 May 2011 within a few hours of one another, all built to the same template and all excerpts. Each carries a site-written synopsis, then a section heading, then the opening formula and the first lines of a lesson, and then breaks off on an ellipsis; the full text sits behind a .doc download in the /medias/doc/L-* series, numbered L-26 to L-39 in the same order as the IDs. The uniform timestamps are a bulk upload and say nothing about when the lesson was delivered.

The record contains two distinct voices and the English keeps them apart. The opening paragraph is a synopsis written by the site, about the lesson and in the third person; everything from the section heading onward is the Sheikh's own words as transcribed. Nothing in the synopsis may be quoted as his.

The source's final line, 'تحميل المادة' ('download the material'), is the label of a download link in the page furniture, not part of the text. It is recorded as source_download_link and omitted from body_ar and body_en.

The base text being commented on is identified inside this run. Record 719 has the Sheikh speaking of 'completing the commentary on the Sheikh's versification', and of that versifier's rendering of Khalil's Jāmiʿ in some five hundred lines; record 716 describes the base text as a versification of the Mukhtaṣar of Khalil ibn Ishaq whose opening section is on creed; and record 718 introduces the same quoted lines with 'the versifier said'. Taken together these settle that 'the Sheikh, may God preserve him' in this run is the living author of the versified base text and not the lecturer. The author is never named.

Unlike the rest of this run, the served portion of this record contains a complete argument in the Sheikh's own voice, ending in his own stated conclusion: the science of the oneness of God is among the most excellent of the sciences, and he declines to call it the most excellent without qualification. Because he does reach his own position, this record is NOT marked critical_for_display, although it remains an excerpt and must still carry the excerpt banner.

The line of al-Maqqari is rendered as prose in italics per style guide section 4; the attribution is kept exactly as given, with no expansion of the name. The same authority is cited in record 713 of this run.
'مسطرة' is a ruler or straightedge; 'lay a measuring rule across them' keeps the image, which is the Sheikh's own.
